title: Case Study: Real-time Streaming Application
interviewAnswer: Describe event source → Kafka → stream processor → storage/cache/API → UI. Explain why streaming was needed, what each component owns, how containers communicate and where failures are observed.
why: This case demonstrates end-to-end data engineering: event ingestion, stateful processing, API/cache, UI, containers and cloud deployment.
intuition: Separate producers from processors with Kafka, compute continuously with Flink, serve recent/aggregated data through an API, cache hot reads, and keep each service independently deployable.
deepDive: Discuss topic/partition design, consumer offsets, event-time vs processing-time, state/checkpoints in Flink, Redis as a cache rather than source of truth, Flask API boundaries, and Docker Compose for local multi-service orchestration. Explain failure recovery and exactly-once/at-least-once claims carefully.
workedExample: Telemetry events → Kafka topic → Flink stateful classification/aggregation → low-latency store/cache → backend API → operational dashboard. Docker Compose can run local versions of the broker, stream processor, cache, backend and frontend as separate services.
commonMistakes: Calling Kafka just a queue and ignoring retention/replay.
Assuming multiple containers always require different images.
Claiming exactly-once end-to-end without checking sinks and commits.
followUps: Why Kafka instead of direct API calls?
What happens when the consumer crashes?
production: Monitor consumer lag, event throughput, checkpoint health, late events, API latency and cache hit rate. Scale partitions/consumers and TaskManagers based on bottlenecks rather than adding replicas blindly.
